paragraphs: Let us put it to them: "Tell us about this statement of yours — is it a statement you arrived at by the senses, or by something else?" If they claim that they reached it by the senses and by direct observation,[{2}] they are asserting something false about the perception and direct observation of mankind, since there is no disparity at all among human beings regarding what is given to the senses.[{3}] And if they claim that they know it otherwise than by the senses, they have annulled their own thesis and acknowledged a knowledge that is not from the senses.

Tell us, then, about someone who enters a house, sees nothing in it, then comes back to find elephants and camels in the house. What is he obligated to conclude? Is he obligated to conclude that the elephants and camels were already in the house when he first entered, only he did not see them? Or that they were not in the house when he first entered? If they say that he is obligated to conclude that the animals were already in the house at the time of his first entry but that he simply did not see them, they have lapsed into self-imposed ignorance,[{4}] and it follows that they do not know whether perhaps elephants and camels are presently in their company that they cannot see — and they have thereby overturned their own first principle (that they affirm nothing except what they have observed), since they have just affirmed what they themselves did not observe: that elephants and camels were in the house on the first entry. But if they say he is obligated to conclude that the elephants and camels were not in the house at the time of his first entry, then ask them: should he conclude that the animals came into being in the house out of nothing, or that they were somewhere else first and then moved into the house? If they answer the second — that they were elsewhere and then moved in — they have once again admitted a knowledge of what they did not witness, and thereby overturned the principle "we know nothing except by observation." For they have not observed the animals moving in, nor have they observed the act of transition, and yet they have affirmed that the animals did move into the house.[{5}]

Ask them about bodies (al-ajsām):[{6}] are they eternal (qadīma) or originated (muḥdatha)? Whichever of the two they choose, they have annulled their own thesis — for they did not observe the bodies' eternity, nor did they observe their coming into being, and yet they have decided in favor of one of the two options without observation. If they say: we do not know whether they are eternal or originated, say to them: do you know, then, that bodies cannot be outside both options (i.e. that they must be one or the other)?[{7}] If they say "yes," ask them: did you know that by observation? If they assert that they did, they have annulled what they said before (namely, "we do not know whether bodies are eternal or originated") [— for the question of whether one of the two must hold is the question itself]. If they say "no, we don't even know that," they have nullified their own admission. We then put it to them: is it possible that bodies are neither eternal nor originated, or is that impossible? Whichever option they assert, ask them: did you know that by sense?[{8}] If they assert that they did, they have lied; if they assert anything else, they have nullified their thesis.[{9}] ---
